stem: Which of the following enzymes is required for synthesis of all eicosanoids?
why: PLA2 cuts arachidonic acid out of membrane phospholipid: the starting step for every eicosanoid.

stem: Prostaglandin E₂ receptor EP₂ is a G_(s)-coupled receptor. What second messenger would be expected in response to PGE₂ in cells expressing EP₂?
why: Gs → adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cAMP.

stem: Which of the following pharmaceutical classes is most likely to cause ulcers in the digestive epithelium?
why: NSAIDs block COX-1 → ↓ protective PGE2 + shunt to LTB4 → ulcers. Coxibs = cardiovascular; glucocorticoids = immunosuppression/catabolism.

stem: Which cell-cycle checkpoint is the go/no-go decision point for cell cycle?
why: G1/S = the most important go/no-go checkpoint ("divide or die").

stem: Growth factor receptors (e.g. EGF receptor) activate which pathway?
why: Receptor tyrosine kinase → SOS → Ras → MAPK.

stem: The G₁/S cyclin-dependent kinase phosphorylates which protein?
why: G1-CDK phosphorylates pRb → E2F released → S phase.

stem: After a cell-cycle checkpoint is completed, what generally happens to the associated cyclin?
opts: It is degraded by the proteasome
It binds to the cyclin-dependent kinase and inactivates it
why: CDK phosphorylates its own cyclin → proteasome, so the cycle can't go back.

stem: Which of the following proteins tends to cause mitochondrial pores to remain closed and reduces the activity of the internal apoptotic pathway?
why: Bcl-2 keeps mitochondrial pores closed → no cytochrome C release. Bax opens them.

stem: A neoplasm that expresses high levels of Fas would likely:
opts: Be very susceptible to immune destruction
Have reduced susceptibility to immune destruction
why: Fas on the tumor = target for FasL on cytotoxic T cells → extrinsic apoptosis → very susceptible. Tumors that EXPRESS FasL kill T cells instead.

stem: Which of the following proteins would be correctly identified as a protooncogene? (select ALL that apply)
why: Gain of activity causes cancer: β-catenin, Bcl-2, E2F, Ras = proto-oncogenes. pRb = tumor suppressor.
flag: β-catenin, Bcl-2 and E2F classified by the gain/loss rule; confirm at review if unsure.

stem: Which of the following proteins would be correctly identified as a tumor suppressor gene? (select ALL that apply)
why: Loss of activity causes cancer: APC, Bax, p21, p53, pRb are all brakes = tumor suppressors. Select-all where every option is correct.

stem: Which of the following could produce extra oxidative stress in a cell? (select ALL that apply)
why: Chronic inflammation (respiratory burst), excess iron (Fenton), reperfusion (reverse electron flow) all raise ROS. Vitamins C and E are antioxidants.

stem: Some pathogenic bacteria (e.g. staphylococcal aureus) express high levels of catalase. High levels of catalase expression could cause which of the following?
opts: Increased susceptibility of the bacteria to oxidative damage
Inability of neutrophils to recognize the bacteria
Reduced metabolic rate of the immune system
Resistance of the bacteria to lysosomal degradation by phagocytes
why: Catalase destroys the phagocyte's H2O2 → bacteria survive inside phagocytes (virulence factor).

stem: An increase in oxidized thioredoxin will activate which signaling pathway?
opts: Glomus cell depolarization – neural signaling pathway
why: Oxidized thioredoxin releases ASK1 (a MAPKKK) → MAPK → hyperoxia genes/apoptosis.

stem: Which of these is an important membrane antioxidant?
why: Vitamin E has a lipid tail → membrane antioxidant. Glutathione = intracellular; vitamin C = blood.

stem: Please explain why Coxibs may potentiate clotting events.
ans: MODEL ANSWER: Coxibs block COX-2 → ↓ endothelial PGI2 (anti-clotting, Gs) while platelet COX-1 still makes TxA2 (pro-clotting, Gq) → balance tips toward clotting → cardiovascular events.
why: Clotting rule: block COX-2 → toward clotting.

stem: What is the K_(d) of Compound A
ctx: You are exploring new treatments for reducing hypoglycemia in insulinoma patients by targeting the glucagon receptor. Compounds A and B bind the glucagon receptor. Use the graphs to answer.
ans: MODEL ANSWER: ~1 µM (50% of glucagon receptors bound).
why: Binding graph: Compound A crosses 50% bound at 1 µM.

stem: What is the K_(d) of Compound B?
why: Binding graph: Compound B crosses 50% bound at ~3 µM (higher KD = lower affinity than A).

stem: What is the EC₅₀ of Compound A?
why: Response runs from ~150 (baseline) to ~550 nM cAMP; halfway (~350) is at ~1 µM. EC50 ≈ KD → no spare receptors.

stem: What is the E_(max) of Compound A?
ans: MODEL ANSWER: ~550 nM cAMP (an increase of ~400 nM over the ~150 nM baseline).
why: Top plateau of the solid curve. Give units of the RESPONSE (nM cAMP), not drug concentration.
flag: Whether Basel wants the plateau (550) or the rise above baseline (400) is unclear; state both.

stem: What type of ligand is Compound B (be as specific as possible)? Why?
ans: MODEL ANSWER: Non-competitive antagonist. It binds the receptor (binding graph) but causes no cAMP alone, and with A it LOWERS Emax (550 → ~375) without a big EC50 shift.
why: Lower ceiling = non-competitive; a right shift with the same ceiling would be competitive.

stem: What is the ED50 of Compound A?
why: Solid (therapeutic) curve crosses 50% of the population at ~3 mg/kg.

stem: What is the LD50 of Compound A?
why: Dotted (life-threatening) curve crosses 50% at ~300 mg/kg.

stem: What is the therapeutic index of Compound A?
why: TI = LD50 / ED50 = 300 / 3 ≈ 100. Ratio = unitless.

stem: Which compound has the higher affinity for the insulin receptor?
ctx: You are investigating ligands of the insulin receptor (compounds 1556, 2334, B): binding studies, skeletal muscle activation (measured as increasing IP3), and in vivo reduction of hyperglycemic events. Use the graphs to answer.
why: Binding graph: 2334 KD ≈ 3 µM vs 1556 KD ≈ 30 µM → lower KD = higher affinity.

stem: Which compound has the higher potency on skeletal muscle cells?
why: EC50: 2334 ≈ 2 µM (half of 400) vs 1556 ≈ 30 µM (half of 650) → lower EC50 = more potent.

stem: Which compound has the higher efficacy on skeletal muscle cells?
why: Emax: 1556 ≈ 650 nM IP3 vs 2334 ≈ 400 → 1556 has higher efficacy.

stem: If insulin (the endogenous agonist) has an E_(max) on your skeletal system of approximately 500 nM IP₃, compound 1556 would best be considered a:
why: 1556 Emax (~650) > insulin's 500 → super agonist.

stem: If insulin (the endogenous agonist) has an E_(max) on your skeletal system of approximately 500 nM IP₃, compound 2334 would best be considered a:
why: 2334 Emax (~400) < insulin's 500 → partial agonist.

stem: You decided not to continue pursuing compound B, because though it bound to the insulin receptor, it didn’t appear to activate the insulin receptor. Based on your studies, compound B would best be considered a:
why: B alone does nothing, but it halves the Emax of both agonists (650 → ~325, 400 → ~200) → non-competitive antagonist.

stem: Do there appear to be spare insulin receptors in skeletal muscle in the system you are using?
why: EC50 ≈ KD for both compounds (1556: ~30 vs ~30; 2334: ~2 vs ~3) → no spare receptors.

stem: What is the E_(max) of compound 1556?
why: Emax is in RESPONSE units: top of the 1556 curve ≈ 625–650 nM IP3.

stem: In your model organism, what was the ED₅₀ of compound 1556?
why: Therapeutic curve crosses 50% at 1 mg/kg.

stem: In your model organism, what was the LD₅₀ of compound 1556?
why: Hypoglycemia curve crosses 50% at ~125 mg/kg.

stem: Estimate the therapeutic index of compound 1556.
why: TI = 125 / 1 = 125 (unitless; the options with units are traps).

stem: During which stage of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
why: DNA replication = S phase.

stem: Which family of proteins act to integrate cell-cycle checkpoint signals?
why: CDKs integrate the checkpoint signals.

stem: Cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) activity require which signal(s)? (select ALL that apply)
opts: Binding to a phase dependent cyclin
Having a kinase add a phosphate
Having a phosphatase remove a phosphate
Having a protease cleave the CDK
why: Cyclin bound + kinase adds a phosphate + phosphatase removes one. No protease cleavage.

stem: A mutation that prevents phosphorylation of β-catenin is likely to lead to:
why: Unphosphorylated β-catenin is never destroyed → always transcribes cyclin D → unregulated division.

stem: Which of the following proteins is important in synthesis of the leukotrienes?
why: 5-LOX makes leukotrienes; PTGS1/2 make prostanoids.

stem: PGI2 production in the endothelium is dependent on which enzyme? (select ALL that apply)
why: Endothelial PGI2 is made by PTGS2 (COX-2) per the lecture framing.
flag: Select-all: Basel ties endothelial PGI2 to COX-2. Some textbooks also credit COX-1 in endothelium; slides win.

stem: What class of drugs selectively inhibits PGI2 synthesis in endothelial cells?
why: Coxibs block COX-2 only → ↓ endothelial PGI2.

stem: G1-CDK phosphorylates which protein to move through the G1/S checkpoint?
why: G1-CDK phosphorylates pRb → E2F released.

stem: Which of the following proteins potentiates apoptosis by causing mitochondrial membrane pores to open?
why: Bax opens mitochondrial pores → cytochrome C → caspase 9.

stem: Mutated AKT (PKB) that gains constitutive activity would lead to _________ __________ in the cell and would potentiate __________.
why: Always-on AKT → ↑ Bcl-2 → cell survival (brakes off).

stem: β-catenin can promote tumorigenesis if it is mutated in a way that prevents phosphorylation by the Axin-GSK3-APC complex. β-catenin would best be considered a(n):
why: Wild-type β-catenin is a proto-oncogene; the mutation that blocks its destruction makes it oncogenic (gain of activity).

stem: Theoretically, could this mutated β-catenin become a viral oncogene?
why: A gain-of-function mutant (like this β-catenin) could be carried by a virus as a viral oncogene.
flag: Viral oncogenes are NOT tested in 2026 (Basel).

stem: Reactive oxygen species are produced in the mitochondria during (select ALL that apply):
why: Normal metabolism (Complexes I and III leak superoxide) and reperfusion (reverse electron flow). During ischemia there is no O2 to make ROS.
flag: Ischemia itself sets up the damage (succinate build-up), but the ROS burst happens at reperfusion.

stem: Which of the following is a protein antioxidant that can activate hyperoxia signaling pathways?
why: Thioredoxin = protein antioxidant whose oxidation releases ASK1 (hyperoxia signaling).

stem: Which of the following pharmaceuticals is known to be metabolized to a reactive oxygen species in the liver?
why: Acetaminophen → cytochrome P450 → NAPQI.

stem: Which of the following would could potentially be a treatment to reduce oxidative damage in the liver?
opts: Ebselen (an experimental drug that mimics GSH)
PFK15-584 (an experimental drug that prevents β-catenin induced transcription)
Q6 (an experimental drug that downregulates HIF-1α)
why: Ebselen mimics glutathione → neutralizes oxidants in the liver.

stem: Which of the following drug classes reduces production of both prostaglandins and leukotrienes?
why: Glucocorticoids ↑ annexin A1 → block PLA2 → both prostaglandins AND leukotrienes ↓.

stem: You are testing a new drug candidate, Substance A. When cells are treated with substance A, signaling through the PGE₂R (EP₂) is reduced. Further examination shows that substance A increases the EC₅₀ of PGE₂ at the PGE₂R (EP₂) without significantly affecting the E_(Max). Based on this information, you would classify Substance A as:
why: EC50 ↑ with Emax unchanged = competitive antagonist.

stem: You are plotting the concentration of a drug in plasma versus time after oral administration. This study would be considered a:
why: Plasma drug concentration over time = what the body does to the drug = pharmacokinetics.

stem: Which of the following proteins integrates cell-cycle checkpoints to make the go/no-go decision on cell cycle?
why: Cyclin-dependent kinases integrate checkpoints.

stem: In cells sensitive to Wnt, mutation of Axin so that it can no longer bind to APC would predispose to:
why: Axin can't bind APC → no destruction complex → β-catenin always on → neoplasia.

stem: Which of the following proteins is important in connecting the DNA Damage Repair pathways to Cell Cycle pathways?
why: p53 links DNA damage (ATM) to the cell cycle (p21 → CDK).

stem: Cytochrome C release from the mitochondria is an important step in:
why: Cytochrome C + Apaf-1 → caspase 9 = internal (intrinsic) pathway.

stem: Based on its activity in the Wnt/Frizzled pathway, wild type β-catenin would be a(n):
why: Normal β-catenin promotes division when it is regulated = proto-oncogene.

stem: Could a mutated β-catenin that lacked a phosphorylation site be a viral oncogene?
why: A gain-of-function β-catenin could be a viral oncogene.
flag: Viral oncogenes are NOT tested in 2026 (Basel).

stem: Which of the following is likely to increase oxidative stress? (select ALL that apply)
why: Chronic infection (respiratory burst), acetaminophen overdose (NAPQI), space travel (ionizing radiation), transient ischemia (reperfusion). Vitamin C is an antioxidant (excess is peed out).

stem: Which of the following is the most important intracellular antioxidant?
why: GSH (glutathione) = "easily the most important intracellular antioxidant."

stem: Which of the following is an important signaling protein for hyperoxia?
opts: Vitamin E [A graph with a line Description automatically generated][A graph with a line Description automatically generated] [A graph with a line Description automatically generated][A graph with a line Description automatically generated] [A graph of pain reduced and death Description automatically generated]
why: Thioredoxin: oxidized form releases ASK1 → hyperoxia signaling.

stem: You are characterizing a new NSAID drug candidate (New NSAID). You have run binding studies, efficacy studies, and dose-response studies on the new drug. Please describe the following (include correct units on all answers):
parts: a. What are the K_(D) of New NSAID at the COX1/PTGS1 and COX2/PTGS2 enzymes?
b. What are the EC₅₀ of New NSAID in the gastric mucosa and in endothelium?
c. What is the E_(Max) of New NSAID in the gastric mucosa and in endothelium?
d. What is the ED₅₀ and LD₅₀ of New NSAID?
e. What is the therapeutic index of New NSAID?
f. Is New NSAID a PTGS1 selective inhibitor, a PTGS2 selective inhibitor, or both equally? Explain.
g. Predict a significant side effect of New NSAID. Explain your prediction.
ans: MODEL ANSWER: (a) KD: COX-1 ≈ 100 ng/mL, COX-2 ≈ 1000 ng/mL. (b) EC50: gastric mucosa ≈ 10 ng/mL; endothelium ≈ 1000 ng/mL. (c) Emax: gastric ↓ PGE2 by ~35 ng/mL (45 → 10); endothelium ↓ PGI2 by ~22 ng/mL (30 → 8). (d) ED50 ≈ 0.1 mg/kg; LD50 ≈ 1000 mg/kg. (e) TI ≈ 10,000 (unitless). (f) PTGS1 (COX-1) selective: 10× lower KD at COX-1 and 100× lower EC50 in gastric mucosa (COX-1 tissue). (g) Gastric ulcers (↓ protective PGE2, shunt to LTB4); also possible bleeding (↓ platelet TxA2).
why: Read KD from the binding graphs (50% bound), EC50 from halfway between the top and bottom plateaus, ED50/LD50 at 50% population.
flag: Gastric EC50 (10) < COX-1 KD (100) suggests spare enzyme capacity/amplification in gastric mucosa.

stem: Which enzyme is common to all eicosanoid synthesis pathways?
why: PLA2 is common to all eicosanoid pathways.

stem: Selective inhibitors of prostaglandin synthase 2 (PTGS2/COX2) can cause which of the following negative side effects?
why: COX-2 selective → ↓ endothelial PGI2 → clotting → cardiovascular events.

stem: Prostaglandin F2α (PGF2α) signaling causes what event in the female reproductive system?
why: PGF2α → luteolysis of the corpus luteum.

stem: Which stage of the cell cycle represents quiescent (currently non-dividing) cells?
why: G0 = quiescent (can be reactivated).

stem: β-catenin is the effector of which growth factor pathway?
why: β-catenin is the effector of the Wnt pathway.

stem: Which of the following proteins is a proto-oncogene?
why: β-catenin = proto-oncogene. APC and GSK-3 are part of the destruction complex (suppressors).

stem: Which of the following proteins is pro-apoptotic signal in the internal apoptosis pathway?
why: Bax = pro-apoptotic (opens pores). Bcl-2 = anti-apoptotic; FADD/FasL = external pathway.

stem: Which of the following proteins is a tumor suppressor gene?
why: Bax = tumor suppressor (loss of apoptosis → cancer). AKT, EGF, Ras = proto-oncogene side.

stem: Mutated forms of which of the following proteins could be a viral oncogene?
why: Ras gain-of-function (can't hydrolyze GTP) is a classic viral oncogene.
flag: Viral oncogenes are NOT tested in 2026 (Basel).

stem: Which of the following proteins catalyzes the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen?
why: Catalase: H2O2 → H2O + O2.

stem: Which of the following might be a potential treatment targeted against hypoxic hepatocellular carcinomas?
opts: Ebselen (an experimental drug that mimics GSH)
PFK15-584 (an experimental drug that prevents β-catenin induced transcription)
Q6 (an experimental drug that downregulates HIF-1α)
why: Hypoxic tumors rely on HIF → downregulating HIF-1α targets them.

stem: Which signal pathway would you expect to be upregulated during reperfusion AFTER resolution of a transient ischemic event?
opts: HIF-1α Use the following graphs to answer questions 13-21:[C:\Users\mbasel\Downloads\Graph 1.jpg][C:\Users\mbasel\Downloads\Graph 2.jpg][C:\Users\mbasel\Downloads\Graph 3.jpg]
why: Reperfusion → ROS burst → oxidized thioredoxin → ASK1 pathway.

stem: The β2-adrenoceptor is a G-protein coupled receptor with a Gs pathway. What second messenger would you expect when the β2-adrenoceptor is activated?
why: Gs → ↑ cAMP.

stem: Salbutamol is a(n) _____________ of the β2-adrenoceptor.
ctx: Use the salbutamol graphs (dose response, concentration response on equine trachealis, binding) to answer.
why: Salbutamol produces relaxation through the receptor = agonist.

stem: Please estimate the EC50 of salbutamol, include the correct units. What does EC50 tell us?
ans: MODEL ANSWER: ~1 nM. Concentration giving half-maximal response (30% relaxation) = potency.
why: Half of the 60% plateau = 30% → 1 nM.

stem: Please estimate the EMax of salbutamol, include the correct units. What does EMax tell us?
ans: MODEL ANSWER: ~60% relaxation. Maximum possible effect = efficacy.
why: Top plateau, in response units.

stem: Please estimate the KD of salbutamol, include the correct units. What does KD tell us?
ans: MODEL ANSWER: ~100 nM. Concentration binding 50% of receptors = affinity (lower = higher affinity).
why: Binding graph crosses 50% at 100 nM.

stem: Please estimate the ED50 of salbutamol, include the correct units.
why: Improved breathing curve crosses 50% at ~0.03.

stem: Please estimate the LD50 of salbutamol, include the correct units. What does LD50 tell us?
ans: MODEL ANSWER: ~10 mg/inhalation. Dose lethal to 50% of the population.
why: Death curve crosses 50% at 10.

stem: Please estimate the therapeutic index of salbutamol, include the correct units. What does the therapeutic index tell us?
ans: MODEL ANSWER: ~300 (10 / 0.03 ≈ 333; unitless). Safety margin between effective and lethal doses; bigger = safer.
why: TI = LD50 / ED50.

stem: Please compare the KD and EC50 of salbutamol. What does this suggest? Explain why.
ans: MODEL ANSWER: EC50 (~1 nM) is far below KD (~100 nM) → full response with only a small fraction of receptors bound → spare receptors (receptor reserve); signaling, not binding, is limiting.
why: EC50 < KD = spare receptors.

stem: Which of the following proteins is important in synthesis of the leukotrienes?
why: 5-LOX → leukotrienes.

stem: PGI2 signaling causes what second messenger in platelets?
why: PGI2 → IP receptor (Gs) on platelets → ↑ cAMP → platelets rest.

stem: What class of drugs selectively inhibits PGI2 synthesis in endothelial cells?
why: Coxibs (COX-2 selective) → ↓ endothelial PGI2.

stem: G1-CDK phosphorylates which protein to move through the G1/S checkpoint?
why: G1-CDK phosphorylates pRb.

stem: Which of the following proteins potentiates apoptosis by causing mitochondrial membrane pores to open?
why: Bax opens mitochondrial pores.

stem: Mutated AKT (PKB) that gains constitutive activity would lead to _________ __________ in the cell and would potentiate __________.
why: Constitutive AKT → ↑ Bcl-2 → cell survival.

stem: Which of the following pharmaceuticals is known to be metabolized to a reactive oxygen species in the liver?
why: Acetaminophen → NAPQI in the liver.

stem: Which of the following could potentially be a treatment to reduce oxidative damage in the liver?
opts: Ebselen (an experimental drug that mimics GSH)
PFK15-584 (an experimental drug that prevents β-catenin induced transcription)
Q6 (an experimental drug that downregulates HIF-1α)
why: Ebselen mimics glutathione.

stem: Which of the following measurements would best be considered part of pharmacokinetics?
opts: The amount of drug bound to a receptor
The amount of drug clearance by the kidney

The magnitude of effect of a drug bound to a receptor [A graph with a line Description automatically generated][A graph with a line Description automatically generated] [A graph with a line drawn on it Description automatically generated]
why: Kidney clearance = elimination (ADME) = pharmacokinetics. Binding and effect = pharmacodynamics.

stem: Salbutamol activates β2-adrenergic receptors, a Gs-linked receptor. What intracellular second messenger do you expect?
why: Gs → ↑ cAMP.

stem: Estimate the EC50 of salbutamol on the trachealis muscle
why: Half of the 60% plateau (30%) at 5 nM.

stem: Estimate the Emax of salbutamol on the trachealis muscle
why: Plateau = 60% relaxation (response units).

stem: Estimate the KD of salbutamol
why: 50% receptors bound at 1000 nM.

stem: Estimate the therapeutic index of inhaled salbutamol.
why: ED50 ≈ 0.01, LD50 ≈ 3 mg/inhalation → TI ≈ 300 (unitless).

stem: You are studying a compound, Practolol, that you have determined binds to β2-adrenergic receptors but does not cause a signaling event. When you repeat the salbutamol concentration response assay in the presence of Practolol, the EC50 shifts to 50 nM. This suggests that Practolol is a _________ in this system.
why: Binds without signaling and shifts EC50 right (5 → 50 nM) = competitive antagonist.

stem: Compare the Concentration Response Study and the Binding Study. What do the results of these two studies suggest?
ans: MODEL ANSWER: EC50 (~5 nM) is ~200× lower than KD (~1000 nM) → maximal relaxation with few receptors bound → spare receptors (receptor reserve); signaling is limiting.
why: EC50 < KD = spare receptors.

stem: Which enzyme is common to all eicosanoid synthesis pathways?
why: PLA2 is common to all eicosanoid pathways. TxA2 isn't even an enzyme.

stem: Eicosanoids are derived from:
why: Eicosanoids come from arachidonic acid.

stem: Injection of exogenous PGF2α into a pregnant cow near the point of implantation will likely induce:
opts: Production of INF-τ by the embryo
Suppression of LH and FSH production by the pituitary
why: PGF2α → luteolysis → progesterone drops → pregnancy lost (abortion).

stem: Gs proteins induce what second messenger?
why: Gs → cAMP.

stem: What is the Emax of this norepinephrine concentration response curve?
why: Top plateau = 16 µM cAMP (response units).

stem: What is the EC50 of this norepinephrine concentration response curve?
why: Half of 16 (8 µM) at ~30 nM norepinephrine.

stem: If curve A (solid line) is the norepinephrine response curve without any antagonists present, which of the concentration response curves suggests the presence of a competitive antagonist?
why: Short dashes: shifted right, same 16 µM ceiling = competitive. Long dashes = lower ceiling (non-competitive).

stem: Serotonin signaling in the synaptic cleft is primarily attenuated by:
why: Serotonin is cleared from the synapse mainly by reuptake through SERT.
flag: Signal-termination question from an older lecture; likely not on 2026 Exam 4.

stem: Which of the following measurements would be considered part of pharmacokinetics?
opts: Concentration of drug that binds 50% of the receptors
Concentration of drug that elicits 50% maximal response
Effective dose of a drug to treat a disease
Plasma concentration of drug over time []
why: Plasma concentration over time = pharmacokinetics.

stem: Approximate the therapeutic index of the experimental anti-MRSA antibiotic MFM501
why: ED50 ≈ 100 mg/kg, LD50 ≈ 2000 mg/kg → TI ≈ 20 (unitless).

stem: During which phase of mitosis do the chromosomes first condense?
why: Chromosomes condense in prophase.

stem: FasL is a signal that activates:
why: FasL → Fas → FADD → caspase 8 = external pathway.

stem: What is often the most damaging component of transient ischemia?
opts: Reduced [ATP] due to loss of H+ gradient
Release of free iron into the cytosol
why: The oxidative burst at reperfusion causes most of the damage.

stem: Which of the following might be a potential treatment for transient ischemia?
opts: Ebselen (an experimental drug that mimics GSH)
PFK15-584 (an experimental drug that prevents β-catenin induced transcription)
Q6 (an experimental drug that downregulates HIF-1α)
why: Ebselen (glutathione mimic) quenches the reperfusion ROS.

stem: What signal pathway would you expect to be upregulated during reperfusion?
why: Reperfusion ROS → oxidized thioredoxin → ASK1.

stem: You are studying the thromboxane A2 receptor (TxA2R) in platelets. During this study you identify an extremely potent agonist called BOP. Upon further study, the potency of this agonist in concentration response studies seems to be significantly greater than its affinity in binding studies. You also identify an irreversible antagonist, I-PTA-PON3, that covalently bonds to TxA2R and inactivates it. Use this information to answer the following questions:
parts: a. What effect do you expect BOP to cause in the platelets (i.e. what effect could you measure)? Please list a final effect (what will happen to the platelet) and a second messenger effect (what intracellular signals you could measure) that you could measure.
b. What quantity describes potency? What quantity describes affinity? Write a mathematical formula that relates these two quantities for BOP in this situation.
c. Why do you think the potency of BOP is significantly higher than the affinity for TxA2R? Propose a mechanism for the enhanced potency.
d. How do you expect the BOP concentration response curve to change if you add a low concentration of I-PTA-PON3 to the solution? (Please refer to EC50 and Emax in your answer)
ans: MODEL ANSWER: (a) TxA2 receptor = Gq → platelet aggregation (final effect); ↑ IP3, DAG, Ca2+ (second messengers). (b) Potency = EC50; affinity = KD; for BOP, EC50 < KD (EC50 << KD). (c) Spare receptors / signal amplification: full response with only a fraction of receptors bound. (d) A low dose of the irreversible antagonist uses up the receptor reserve: EC50 shifts RIGHT with Emax unchanged (looks competitive); at higher doses Emax falls.
why: Combines LC28 (TxA2 = Gq, aggregation) with LC30 spare receptors.

stem: APC is a protein that binds both to β-catenin and the Axin/GSK3 complex and allows Axin/GSK3 to phosphorylate β-catenin. Use this information to answer the following questions:
parts: a. What growth factor pathway is APC associated with?
b. How does signaling through this pathway affect APC?
c. What happens to phosphorylated β-catenin? If β-catenin is not phosphorylated, what does it do?
d. Mutations in APC that prevent APC from interacting with Axin/GSK3 would cause what effect in a cell?
e. Based on this information, is wild-type APC an oncogene, a proto-oncogene, or a tumor-suppressor gene?
f. If a mutated APC that could not interact with Axin/GSK3 was encoded by a retrovirus, would this retrovirus be oncogenic? Why or why not?
ans: MODEL ANSWER: (a) Wnt. (b) Wnt → Frizzled/LRP → Dishevelled pulls APC off the Axin/GSK3 complex → no phosphorylation of β-catenin. (c) Phosphorylated β-catenin → proteasome; unphosphorylated β-catenin enters the nucleus and transcribes cyclin D → cell cycling. (d) β-catenin never phosphorylated → always on → unregulated division/neoplasia. (e) Tumor suppressor (cancer from LOSS of activity). (f) Probably not: a loss-of-function APC carried by a virus doesn't remove the cell's own working APC, so it wouldn't act as an oncogene.
why: Part (f) is a viral-oncogene question.
flag: Viral oncogenes (part f) are NOT tested in 2026.

stem: Which enzyme releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, initiating eicosanoid synthesis?
why: PLA₂ cuts arachidonic acid out of the membrane: the first step for every eicosanoid. COX and 5-LOX act after.

stem: Which platelet-derived eicosanoid mediates platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction?
why: TxA₂ = platelets (COX-1), Gq → clot + constrict. PGI₂ is its opposite (endothelium, Gs).

stem: Why can selective COX-2 inhibitors (Coxibs) increase the risk of thrombotic events?
opts: They reduce endothelial PGI₂ without reducing TxA₂
They inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2 equally
why: Endothelial PGI₂ is COX-2; platelet TxA₂ is COX-1. Block only COX-2 → anti-clot signal lost, pro-clot signal stays.

stem: A hypovolemic patient develops acute kidney injury after NSAID administration. What mechanism explains this?
opts: Loss of PGI₂-mediated increased renin release
Enhanced TXA₂ synthesis leading to thrombotic events
Loss of PGE₂-mediated afferent arteriolar dilation
Increased aldosterone sensitivity and efferent arteriolar constriction
why: Low volume → kidney leans on PGE₂ to dilate the afferent arteriole and hold GFR. NSAID removes it → AKI.

stem: Why are eicosanoids typically autocrine or paracrine rather than endocrine signals?
opts: They are synthesized in the Golgi apparatus.
They are hydrophobic and lack carrier proteins.
They circulate tightly bound to plasma proteins.
They are secreted in vesicles and stored.
why: Lipid, made on demand, no carrier, short-lived → acts locally.

stem: Why can the same prostaglandin both protect the stomach and promote inflammation elsewhere?
opts: Its concentration threshold for receptor binding differs among tissues.
Different tissues express receptor subtypes coupled to distinct second-messenger pathways.
Cytokine expression modifies prostaglandin degradation rate.
COX-1 and COX-2 produce stereoisomers with opposite effects.
why: PGE₂ hits EP subtypes: EP2 = Gs, EP3 = Gi. Same ligand, different receptor → different effect.

stem: A β₂-adrenergic agonist initially causes bronchodilation but becomes less effective after chronic use. Which mechanism explains this?
opts: Receptor internalization and reduced signaling efficiency
Increased receptor affinity reducing available agonist
Decreased adenylyl cyclase activity from low cAMP
why: Desensitization: GRK phosphorylates → arrestin → receptor internalized (downregulation).

stem: What advantage do second messengers like cAMP provide to signaling systems?
opts: Allow amplification and integration of signals
why: One receptor → many cAMP → many PKA: amplification; several inputs converge: integration.

stem: Clenbuterol and albuterol are both β₂-adrenoceptor agonists, but clenbuterol has an EC50 of ~5nM while albuterol has an EC50 of ~0.5nM. Based on this data, clenbuterol is ______ relative to albuterol.
why: Higher EC50 = more drug needed = LESS potent. EC50 says nothing about efficacy (Emax).

stem: Morphine and buprenorphine have different maximal effects on the μ-opioid system, with buprenorphine's maximum effect being approximately 50% of morphine's maximal effect. Compared to morphine, buprenorphine would be considered a:
why: Lower Emax than the full agonist = partial agonist.

stem: Pharmacokinetics is best summarized as:
opts: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination of the drug
why: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME). PD = what the drug does to the body.

stem: The KD for a ligand represents:
opts: The concentration producing 50% of the maximal response
The concentration causing toxic effects in 50% of subjects
The concentration that doubles signal amplification
The concentration where half of receptors are bound
why: KD = 50% receptors bound (binding graph). Trap: 50% max response = EC50; 50% toxic = TD50.

stem: During which phase of the cell cycle has DNA already been duplicated, but mitosis not yet occurred?
why: S copies DNA; G₂ is the gap after S and before M.

stem: In the Wnt/Frizzled pathway, what happens to β-catenin in the absence of Wnt signaling?
opts: Enters the nucleus as a transcription factor
Acts as a phosphorylase, inhibiting transcription pathways
Acts as a kinase, activating transcription pathways
Is targeted to the proteosome for degradation
why: No Wnt → Axin/GSK3/APC complex phosphorylates β-catenin → ubiquitin → proteasome.

stem: Which of these proteins is central to signal integration and progression through cell cycle checkpoints?
why: Basel's slide title: 'Cyclin Dependent Kinases Integrate Checkpoints.' Cyclins activate CDKs; CDK does the integrating.

stem: E2F activation tends to push the cell toward:
why: E2F = transcription factor for S-phase genes → DNA synthesis (G1→S), not mitosis.

stem: Mutations in retinoblastoma protein that prevent E2F binding would tend to promote:
why: pRb is the brake holding E2F. Can't bind E2F → E2F always free → cell keeps cycling.

stem: What tends to happen to cyclins immediately after moving through a checkpoint?
opts: They tend to be phosphorylated to increase activity
They tend to be dephosphorylated to decrease activity
They tend to be proteolytically degraded
They tend to increase in concentration
why: Cyclins are destroyed (ubiquitin → proteasome) after their checkpoint so the cycle moves one way.

stem: Which description distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis?
opts: Rapid lysis and leakage of contents
why: Apoptosis = orderly: DNA fragments, blebs, no inflammation. The others are necrosis.

stem: Which protein inhibits the internal apoptotic pathway by closing mitochondrial pores?
why: Bcl-2 closes pores (anti-apoptotic). Bax opens them. Apaf-1 + caspase 9 = apoptosome.

stem: In the extrinsic apoptosis pathway, which event is central to apoptosis initiation?
why: Extrinsic = external: FasL binds Fas → trimerizes → caspase 8. Cytochrome c is intrinsic; caspase 3 is the shared executioner, not the initiator.

stem: Mutated β-catenin that cannot be phosphorylated by Axin/GSK3/APC and is therefore constitutively active will most likely:
why: Never tagged for destruction → always in nucleus → cyclin D ↑ → more cycling (colon cancer).

stem: Normal (WT/non-mutated) β-catenin would most correctly be considered a(n):
why: Normal gas pedal = proto-oncogene. Mutated always-on version = oncogene.

stem: p21 inhibits CDK2 as part of the p53 DNA damage response pathway. Normal (non-mutated) p21 would most correctly be considered a(n):
why: p21 is a brake on CDK → tumor suppressor. (Confirms the p21 classification.)

stem: Which conditions would most likely increase oxidative damage in tissues? (select ALL that apply)
why: Selenium deficiency → glutathione peroxidase fails; iron → Fenton → •OH; reperfusion → ROS burst. Antioxidants lower damage.

stem: The treatment of acetaminophen toxicity in cats with N-acetylcysteine is effective because it:
opts: Directly oxidizes NAPQI to a harmless metabolite.
Inhibits cytochrome P450 metabolism of acetaminophen.
Replenishes glutathione stores used to detoxify reactive NAPQI.
Chelates iron to prevent hydroxyl radical formation.
why: NAC supplies cysteine → rebuilds glutathione, which conjugates NAPQI.

stem: Which small-molecule antioxidant would most effectively terminate radical chain reactions in lipid membranes?
why: Vitamin E is lipid-soluble → sits in membranes, stops lipid peroxidation chains. Vitamin C is water-soluble (recycles E).

stem: Under hypoxic conditions, HIF-1α levels rise primarily because:
opts: Prolyl hydroxylase requires oxygen to target HIF-1α for degradation.
why: Normal O₂: prolyl hydroxylase tags HIF → VHL → proteasome. No O₂ → no tag → HIF builds up.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the function of the glomus cell in the carotid body?
opts: Hypoxia closes K⁺ channels, depolarizing the cell
Hyperoxia opens K⁺ channels, hyperpolarizing the cell.
Normoxia activates HIF-1α transcription of glycolytic genes.
Hypoxia opens K⁺ channels to reduce cell excitability.
why: Low O₂ → K⁺ channels close → depolarize → Ca²⁺ in → neurotransmitter → ↑ breathing.

stem: Vibrio alginolyticus can express high levels of superoxide dismutase. Strains of V. alginolyticus that express sodB (superoxide dismutase) are likely to:
opts: Be more virulent (more resistant to phagocytic degradation)
Be less virulent (less resistant to phagocytic degradation)
why: Phagocytes kill with superoxide (respiratory burst). Bacterial SOD destroys it → survives inside phagocytes → more virulent.

stem: Estimate the KD of isoproterenol
ctx: Use the graphs (cAMP response, population response, % β1R bound) to answer Q31–Q36.
why: Binding graph (% β1R bound): isoproterenol crosses 50% at ~5 nM. Unit trap: KD is a concentration from the BINDING graph.

stem: Estimate the EC50 of isoproterenol
why: cAMP graph: response runs ~55→155 µM, midpoint ~105 µM at ~2 nM. Trap: mg/kg is ED50 (whole-animal).

stem: Does it appear that there are spare β1-adrenoceptors in cardiomyocytes?
why: EC50 (~2 nM) < KD (~5 nM): full response before half the receptors are bound → spare receptors.

stem: What type of ligand is propranolol in the β1-adrenoceptor system?
why: It binds β1R (binding graph) and shifts the isoproterenol curve RIGHT with the SAME max → competitive antagonist.

stem: Estimate the ED50 of isoproterenol.
why: Population graph: 50% resolution of bradyarrhythmia at ~0.5 mg/kg. ED50 = dose (mg/kg), not concentration.

stem: Estimate the therapeutic index of isoproterenol.
why: TI = LD50 ÷ ED50 = ~50 mg/kg ÷ 0.5 mg/kg = 100. Unitless, so the mg/kg options are traps.
